title: None, without, and amounts: dopełniacz
goal: Use the noun form that comes after negation, amounts, and the prepositions *do*, *od*, *bez*, *dla* — the second most important form after *biernik*.

dialogs.title: Dialogue — W sklepie
dialogs.intro: A small corner grocery. A short line; it's Budi's turn.

lines.speaker: Sprzedawczyni:
lines.id: Good afternoon, what can I get you?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Poproszę kilo jabłek i pół kilo pomidorów.
lines.id: A kilo of apples and half a kilo of tomatoes, please.
lines.literal: I-ask kilo apples and half kilo tomatoes.

lines.speaker: Sprzedawczyni:
lines.text: Niestety nie ma. Mamy tylko zwykłe.
lines.id: Unfortunately not. We only have regular.
lines.literal: unfortunately not is. we-have only regular.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: To poproszę dwa litry zwykłego. I bochenek chleba.
lines.id: Then two liters of regular. And a loaf of bread.
lines.literal: so I-ask two liters regular. and loaf bread.

lines.speaker: Sprzedawczyni:
lines.text: Chleb się skończył. Będzie po drugiej.
lines.id: The bread's run out. There'll be more after two.
lines.literal: bread self finished. will-be after second.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Szkoda. W takim razie to wszystko. Ile płacę?
lines.id: Shame. In that case, that's everything. How much do I owe?
lines.literal: pity. in such case this everything. how-much I-pay?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Here you go. Sorry, I don't have small change.

lines.speaker: Sprzedawczyni:
lines.text: Nie szkodzi. Proszę resztę i paragon.
lines.id: No problem. Here's your change and the receipt.
lines.literal: not harms. please change and receipt.

notes: **Nie ma is the most important phrase in this unit.** It means "there isn't / there's no" and is **always** followed by the *dopełniacz* form: *nie ma chleba*, *nie ma czasu*, *nie ma problemu*. It never changes for anything — one chunk for every situation.

**Negation shifts the ending.** *Mam czas* → *Nie mam czasu*. *Piję kawę* → *Nie piję kawy*. Every object that was in *biernik* moves to *dopełniacz* as soon as the sentence is negated. This rule has no exceptions — and nothing like it exists in English.

**Kilo jabłek, pół kilo pomidorów.** Amounts take this form too, and here it's **plural**: *jabłka → jabłek*, *pomidory → pomidorów*. The plural ending is *-ów* for masculine words, and often **no ending at all** for feminine and neuter words (*jabłka → jabłek*, *książki → książek*).

**Bez laktozy, do sklepu, od mamy, dla ciebie** — the four most common prepositions, and all four take *dopełniacz*. Know just these four and you're already using this form correctly dozens of times a day.
**Chleb się skończył** — "the bread's run out", literally "the bread finished itself". You'll hear it often in shops and bakeries toward the afternoon.
**Będzie po drugiej** — *będzie* is the future form of *być*: "there will be". The full future comes in unit 19; *będzie* alone is worth learning now because it's used so much.
**Nie szkodzi** — "no problem, never mind", the standard reply to a small apology. Its siblings: *nic się nie stało* (nothing happened) and *w porządku* (it's fine).
**W takim razie** — "in that case", a linking phrase that makes you sound far more advanced than your grammar really is. Use it as often as you can.

grammars.title: Dopełniacz — the endings
body: The form that answers *kogo? czego?* — "there's no what", "how much of what", "whose".
after: **Feminine** words take **-y** (or **-i** after a soft letter). **Neuter** words always take **-a**. **Masculine** words take **-a** or **-u**, and there's no rule you can really rely on — living beings almost always get *-a*, things can go either way.

An honest shortcut for masculine words: learn the *do…* form together with each new word. *Sklep → do sklepu*, *dom → do domu*, *dworzec → do dworca*. Since *do* is used so often, the right form will stick through habit.
The plural: **-ów** for masculine words (*pomidorów*, *biletów*), and **no ending** for many feminine and neuter words (*jabłek*, *książek*, *piw*).

grammars.title: Four uses you must recognize
body: This form shows up in four situations, and all four often come up in the same conversation.

head: Situation
Example
English
rows: Lots of work. A kilo of apples.

after: The last row explains something that often confuses learners: Polish puts the owner **after** the thing — "brother's car" is *samochód brata*, literally "car of-brother". It works like English "the car of my brother", never like "brother's car".

⚠️ *Dużo*, *mało*, *trochę*, *ile* all take this form: *dużo czasu*, *mało pieniędzy*, *trochę mleka*, *ile wody*. It's one of the quickest giveaways of a foreigner who's got it versus one who hasn't.

blocks.text: ⚠️ *Deko* is a typically Polish measure: one *deko* = 10 grams. At the meat and cheese counter people order *dwadzieścia deko* (200 grams), not grams. Saying grams will be understood, but it sounds like reading a label.

blocks.title: Three things that surprise newcomers in Polish shops
items: **Plastic bags cost extra.** You'll always be asked first, and Poles almost always bring their own bags.
**You weigh fruit and vegetables yourself** in big supermarkets, including typing the product number into the scale. In small shops, the seller does the weighing.
**Small shops close early** and many are closed on Sundays — Poland has restricted Sunday trading in recent years. Look for *niedziela handlowa* (trading Sunday) before planning a shopping trip.
